questions.q:
Rate law for a reaction between A and B is given by
$\mathrm{R}=\mathrm{k}[\mathrm{~A}]^{\mathrm{n}}[\mathrm{~B}]^{\mathrm{m}}$
If concentration of A is doubled and concentration of $B$ is halved from their initial value, the ratio of new rate of reaction to the initial rate of reaction \left(\frac{r_2}{r_1}\right)$ is$
questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{r}_1=\mathrm{k}[\mathrm{~A}]^{\mathrm{n}}[\mathrm{~B}]^{\mathrm{m}}$
Now A is doubled \& B is halved in concentration
$\Rightarrow \mathrm{r}_2=\mathrm{k} 2^{\mathrm{n}}[\mathrm{~A}]^{\mathrm{n}} \cdot \frac{[\mathrm{~B}]^{\mathrm{m}}}{2^{\mathrm{m}}}$
Now $\frac{r_2}{r_1}=2^{(n-m)}$

questions.q:
The following results were obtained during kinetic studies of the reaction.

$2A + B \to$ product
~
Experiment \left[A\right] \left(inmolL^{- 1}\right)$ \left[$B\right] \left($inmolL^{- 1}\right)$ Initial rate of reaction \left(inmolL^{- 1}min{ }^{- 1}\right)$
$I$ $0 . 10$ $0 . 20$ $6.93 \times {10}^{- 3}$
$II$ $0 . 10$ $0 . 25$ $6.93 \times {10}^{- 3}$
$III$ $0 . 20$ $0 . 30$ $1.386 \times {10}^{- 2}$

The time (in minutes) required to consume half of $\text{A}$is$
questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.solution:
Let's& assume $x$ and $y$ are the order of the reaction with respect to~$A$ and $B$,~respectively.

From equation \left(1\right)$ and \left(2\right)$,

\left(\dfrac{0 .1}{0 .1}\right)x\left(\dfrac{0 .2}{0 .25}\right)y = \dfrac{6 .93 \times {10}^{- 3}}{6 .93 \times {10}^{- 3}} ⇒ y = 0$

From equation \left(1\right)$ and \left(3\right)$ and put the value $y = 0$,

\left(\dfrac{0 .1}{0 .2}\right)x\left(\dfrac{0 .2}{0 .3}\right)0 = \dfrac{6 .93 \times {10}^{- 3}}{1 .386 \times {10}^{- 2}}∴ y = 0$

\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)x = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) ⇒ x = 1$

The rate law will be $R = K{[ A ]}^{1}{[ B ]}^{0}$

Hence, the reaction is of the first order.

$K = R\left[A\right] = \dfrac{6 .93 \times {10}^{- 3}}{0 .1} = 6 .93 \times {10}^{- 2}$

Here $t\dfrac{1}{2}$ for~the first-order reaction is given by,~$t\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{0 .693}{K} = \dfrac{0 .693}{( 6 .93 \times {10}^{- 2})} =10

questions.q: A flask contains a mixture of compounds $A$ and $B$. Both compounds decompose by first-order kinetics. The half-lives for $A$ and $B$ are $300s$ and $180s$, respectively. If the concentrations of $A$ and $B$ are equal initially, the time required for the concentration of A to be four times that of $B$~(in s) is : $( Useln2 = 0 . 693 )$
questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.solution:
${C}_{t} = {C}_{0}e^{- kt}$

${k}_{A} = \dfrac{ln2}{300}$~ ~ ~ \left(k = \dfrac{ln2}{T1 / 2}\right)$

${k}_{B} = \dfrac{ln2}{180}$

\left({C}_{t}\right)A = \left({C}_{0}\right)Ae^{- {k}_{A}t}$~ ~ ~

\left({C}_{t}\right)B = \left({C}_{0}\right)Be^{- {k}_{B}t}$

$\dfrac{\left({C}_{t}\right), B}{\left({C}_{t}\right), A} = \dfrac{\left({C}_{0}\right), B}{\left({C}_{0}\right), A} \times e^{\left({k}_{A} - {k}_{B}\right)t}$

$\dfrac{1}{4} = e^{\left({k}_{A} - {k}_{B}\right)t}$

$ln\dfrac{1}{4} = \left[\dfrac{ln2}{300} - \dfrac{ln2}{180}\right]t$

$- 2ln2 = \left[\dfrac{ln2}{300} - \dfrac{ln2}{180}\right]t$

$2 = \left(\dfrac{120}{180 \times 300}\right)t$

$t = \dfrac{2 \times 180 \times 300}{120} = 900sec$

$

questions.q: In a reaction $A+B \rightarrow C$, initial concentrations of $A$ and $B$ are related as $[A]_0=8[B]_0$. The half lives of $A$ and $B$ are 10 min and 40 min. respectively. If they start to disappear at the same time, both following first order kinetics, after how much time will the concentration of both the reactants be same?
questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.solution:
Given : $[\mathrm{A}]_0=8[\mathrm{~B}]_0$
\left[\mathrm{t}_{1 / 2}\right]_{\mathrm{A}}=10 \mathrm{~min}$.
\left[\mathrm{t}_{1 / 2}\right]_{\mathrm{B}}=40 \mathrm{~min}$.
$\mathrmI^{\text {st }}$ order kinetics
$\mathrm{t}=$ ?
$[\mathrm{A}]_{\mathrm{t}}=[\mathrm{B}]_{\mathrm{t}}$
$-\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{A}} \times \mathrm{t} \quad-\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{B}} \times \mathrm{t}$
$\Rightarrow \quad[\mathrm{A}]_0 \mathrm{e}=[\mathrm{B}]_0 \mathrm{e}$
$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{~B}]_0}=\mathrme^{\left(\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{A}}-\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{B}}\right) \mathrm{t}}$
$\Rightarrow \quad 8=\mathrme^{\left(\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{A}}-\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{B}}\right) \times \mathrm{t}}$
$\Rightarrow \quad \ell \mathrm{n} 8=\left(\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{A}}-\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{B}}\right) \times \mathrm{t}$
$\Rightarrow \quad \ln 8=\ln 2\left(\frac{1}{\left(\operatorname{ta}_2\right)_{\mathrm{A}}}-\frac{1}{\left(\operatorname{ta}_2\right)_{\mathrm{B}}}\right) \times \mathrm{t}$

$- \dfrac{\Delta\left[{N}_{2}{O}_{5}\right]}{Δt} = - \dfrac{( 2 . 75 - 3 )}{30 - 0}molL^{- 1}\min^{- 1} = \dfrac{0 . 25}{30}$

$≃ 17 \times {10}^{- 3}M / Min$

questions.q: A molecule undergoes two independent first order reactions whose respective half lives are $12min$ and $3min$. If both the reactions are occurring then the time taken for the $50 %$ consumption of the reactant is ______ $min$. (Nearest integer)
questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.solution:
For parallel reaction

When adding the rate constants of the two reactions, we need to use the formula for combining rate constants of two reactions in parallel, which is:

$k = {k}_{1} + {k}_{2}$

where ${k}_{1}$ and ${k}_{2}$ are the rate constants of the individual reactions.

In this case, the half-lives of the two reactions are $12$ min and $3$ min, respectively. The rate constants of the two reactions can be calculated using the formula for half-life of a first-order reaction:

$\dfrac{1}{t1 / 2} = \dfrac{1}{12} + \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{5}{12}$

Net~${t}_{1 / 2} = \dfrac{12}{5} = 2 . 4min \approx 2min$

Hence time taken for $50 %$ consumption of reactant will be close to $2min$.
